title: Washington LIHEAP 2026-27: How to Get Energy Bill Help
desc: Washington LIHEAP helps with utility bills, unsafe heating units and weatherization through local agencies. How to book your appointment and what it covers.
h1: Washington Heating Help 2026-27: How LIHEAP Works
lead: Washington helps lower-income households with energy bills through its Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program, or LIHEAP. You do not apply to the state. You book an appointment with the agency that serves your county. Here is what the state says it can cover and how to start.

sections: What the program offers

Washington's Department of Commerce runs LIHEAP through community action agencies and local partners. Depending on your situation you may get help with a utility bill, help repairing or replacing an unsafe or inoperative heating or cooling unit, and weatherization through the state's Weatherization Program, which makes the home more energy efficient.
Who decides

Commerce does not decide who qualifies or hand out grants to households. The local agency does. Eligibility depends on your heating costs, your household income and your household size. The state posts eligibility guidelines in a PDF on its page. We did not copy dollar limits here because the page text did not include them.
How to book

You must schedule an appointment with an organization that serves your area. Commerce provides a public map. Pick your county, and the tool shows the contact details for the agency and how to schedule. The state lists a contact for questions at LIHEAP@commerce.wa.gov and 360-725-2857.
The dates

The page was last updated on September 15, 2026 and gives no season start or end date, so we mark this as general information, not as open or closed. Call your agency to ask when appointments are available and what documents to bring.
What to bring
Bring proof of income for everyone in your home, a recent energy bill and photo ID. Agencies may ask for more, so ask at booking. If you rent, bring a lease or a note showing how heat is paid.
A longer fix
Weatherization appears in the same program for a reason: it lowers use. For rebates on heat pumps, thermostats and appliances, see the Washington pages below.
Why we show no season dates

Some states post a clear start and end date. Washington's page does not. It was last updated on September 15, 2026 and describes a year-round network of agencies. Because we cannot promise that money is open or closed, we label the page information, not a program with a deadline. If you need help today, call your county agency and ask about the next open appointment.
Renters and small landlords

The state lists help with repairing or replacing an unsafe or inoperative heating or cooling unit. If you rent, ask the agency whether they will work with your landlord on a broken unit. If you are a small landlord with a tenant who cannot pay, ask the agency how payments reach the utility. We did not read any state rule on this, so confirm before you act.
Keep records

After any visit, write down the date, the agency, the person you spoke with and what you were told to bring. If you are denied, ask for the reason in writing and ask how to appeal. A short record keeps your next call short.
Ask about language help
Local agencies serve many languages. When you book, ask whether they can use an interpreter or translated forms so that nothing is lost.

faq: How do I apply for LIHEAP in Washington?
You schedule an appointment with the agency that serves your county, using the public map tool on the Commerce page.
Does Commerce decide who gets help?
No. Commerce says it does not determine eligibility or award grants to households. Local agencies do.
What can LIHEAP help with in Washington?
Utility bills, repair or replacement of an unsafe or inoperative heating or cooling unit, and weatherization.
Your heating costs, household income and household size.
